post_text:
I watched my best team member walk toward a cliff.

I knew exactly how to stop them, but I kept my mouth shut.

They were building a new process from scratch.

I saw the flaws in their logic immediately.

My instinct was to take the pen and redraw the map.

I wanted to save the schedule and avoid the inevitable mess.

But I remembered how I actually learned this craft.

I didn't learn by being told the right answer.

I learned by feeling the weight of a wrong decision.

So I sat in the back of the room and listened.

I let them lead the meeting.

I let them defend a choice I knew would fail within a month.

Three weeks later, the cracks appeared.

The system they built started to wobble under pressure.

They came to me, not asking for a fix, but with a plan to pivot.

Their confidence didn't break; it hardened through the struggle.

If I had stepped in early, I would have saved a week of work.

Instead, I would have cost them their growth.

Being a leader isn't about being right every time.

It is about creating the space for others to be wrong safely. 🛡️
lesson_extracted: True mentorship requires the discipline to let someone fail when the cost of the mistake is lower than the cost of their professional growth.
